claim: In v0.7, llm-d renamed its core component to the 'llm-d Router' -- defined as 'the functional combination of a Proxy and an Endpoint Picker (EPP)' -- explicitly because the prior terminology ('inference scheduler', 'inference gateway') conflicted with Kubernetes scheduling concepts and was too narrowly tied to the Gateway API; the repository was renamed to llm-d/llm-d-router.
stance_target: identity and scope of the component the user wants to customize
quoted_support: we are renaming the core component to the llm-d Router — the functional combination of a Proxy and an Endpoint Picker (EPP). This replaces the previous "inference scheduler" and "inference gateway" terminology, which conflicted with Kubernetes scheduling concepts and was too narrowly tied to the Gateway API. The repository has been renamed to llm-d-router.

claim: v0.7 makes 'Standalone Mode' the default llm-d deployment, running with a generic proxy (Envoy) instead of requiring the full Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE) stack, letting users 'go from clone to serving in minutes' before layering on gateway features.
stance_target: llm-d has already loosened the router's coupling to the full GAIE/Gateway API stack, though standalone mode still assumes Kubernetes-deployed pods
scope_conditions: llm-d v0.7 release, default deployment mode
quoted_support: The default deployment now runs in standalone mode using a generic proxy (Envoy), rather than requiring the full Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE) stack. You can go from clone to serving in minutes, and layer on gateway features as your deployment matures.

claim: The llm-d v0.8 roadmap (as announced in the v0.7 blog) explicitly includes a 'Non-Kubernetes deployment mode' that 'enables llm-d in Slurm clusters and research labs through file-based service discovery', under the Reinforcement Learning infrastructure workstream.
stance_target: llm-d itself is planning first-party non-Kubernetes backend support via file-based service discovery, directly relevant to router customization for non-k8s backends
scope_conditions: announced as v0.8 roadmap item in the v0.7 blog post; tracked at github.com/llm-d/llm-d/issues/1520
quoted_support: Non-Kubernetes deployment mode enables llm-d in Slurm clusters and research labs through file-based service discovery.

claim: The v0.8 roadmap also plans for NIXL to receive TTL-based cache eviction and request draining for graceful pod termination, and for KV transfer connectors to expand beyond NVIDIA to include Mooncake (Alibaba) and MoRI (Microsoft).
stance_target: upcoming NIXL/connector roadmap relevant to backend diversity
scope_conditions: v0.8 roadmap, announced in v0.7 blog
quoted_support: NIXL (NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library) receives TTL-based cache eviction and request draining for graceful pod termination. KV transfer connectors expand beyond NVIDIA with Mooncake (Alibaba) and MoRI (Microsoft) integrations.

claim: v0.7 migrated the entire llm-d installation surface from Helm/Helmfile to Kustomize, deprecating the llm-d-infra and llm-d-modelservice Helm charts, with every well-lit-path guide now using Kustomize bases and per-platform overlays (GKE, OpenShift, etc.).
stance_target: deployment tooling remains Kubernetes-native even as flexibility increases
quoted_support: The entire installation surface has been migrated from Helm and Helmfile to Kustomize. Every deployment guide... now uses Kustomize bases with per-platform overlays for GKE, OpenShift, and other Kubernetes distributions. The previous llm-d-infra and llm-d-modelservice Helm charts are deprecated.

claim: v0.7 introduced Flow Control as an experimental feature: centralized request queuing and admission control at the Router level, classifying requests by a FlowKey (Fairness ID + Priority), with EPP maintaining per-flow in-memory queues dispatched by priority, fairness, and ordering, integrating with InferenceObjective resources for SLO enforcement.
stance_target: router-level scheduling logic that a non-k8s-aware router customization would need to replicate or preserve
quoted_support: Flow Control moves request queuing to the llm-d Router, enabling intelligent admission control before requests reach model servers. Incoming requests are classified by a FlowKey combining Fairness ID and Priority. The Endpoint Picker (EPP) maintains separate in-memory queues for each flow and dispatches based on three criteria: priority..., fairness..., and ordering...

claim: v0.7's new Architecture Reference documentation covers EPP design (scheduling, flow control, request handling), KV management subsystems (KV Indexer, KV Offloader, routing plugin integration), and a new API reference documenting EPP HTTP headers, EndpointPickerConfig, InferenceModelRewrite, InferenceObjective, and InferencePool resources with concrete examples.
stance_target: primary documentation surface a router customization project should read closely
quoted_support: Architecture Reference: Full coverage of EPP design (scheduling, flow control, request handling), KV management subsystems (KV Indexer, KV Offloader, routing plugin integration)... A new API reference section documents EPP HTTP headers, EndpointPickerConfig, InferenceModelRewrite, InferenceObjective, and InferencePool resources with concrete examples.

claim: v0.7 required a breaking CUDA upgrade from 12.9.1 to 13.0.2 (NVIDIA driver 580+ required) to support Blackwell-generation hardware including a dedicated llm-d-cuda-gb200 image, and bumped vLLM to 0.19.1 (neuralmagic fork).
quoted_support: We have updated from CUDA 12.9.1 to 13.0.2—a breaking change requiring NVIDIA driver 580 or later. This unlocks first-class support for Blackwell-generation hardware, including a dedicated llm-d-cuda-gb200 Docker image...vLLM to 0.19.1 (now tracking the neuralmagic fork with targeted NaN-fix cherry-picks)

claim: v0.7 represented a 3.5x increase in pull request volume over v0.6, with 23 new contributors including hardware vendors Rebellions, Intel, and AMD.
quoted_support: This release represents a 3.5× increase in pull request volume over v0.6... 23 new contributors in this release alone, with hardware vendor contributions from Rebellions, Intel, and AMD
